sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

Case F16: segment the fibrous soft-tissue tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 82x82x58 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case F16 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(82, 82, 58) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: fibrous soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).
axial 29/58 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 1/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking: The volume seems small, suggesting this is a foot or hand, so I'll go with sheets for sizing.

sheet coronal 10–72/82 (16 slices) | v0 | tool calls 3/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm looking at a hand scan with axial slices through the fingers, and the volume dimensions seem oddly magnified for a 1mm scale. Around slices 38-49 I'm noting a fan-like intermediate structure near the palm with dark nodules, possibly a lobulated branching mass with intermediate signal intensity that could represent the lesion.

Could this be fibromatosis or a giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath — hard to say for certain. I'm reconsidering the crop dimensions, wondering if the 82mm volume is centered on the lesion itself, and trying to work out whether the bright round structures near axial slice 29 could be toes, tendons, or nodules based on their size relative to the scale bar. I think I need to examine the center slices more carefully alongside the sagittal views to pin down what these bright structures actually represent.

content.text: sheet sagittal 20–62/82 (12 slices) | v0 | tool calls 4/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm trying to work out the anatomy in these slices—the early axial images look like toe cross-sections with bone marrow visible at center, while the later ones around slice 27-30 show bright oval structures that could be metatarsal heads, with the brightness likely reflecting fat-sensitive T2 fast spin echo signal from marrow.

In the 38-49 range I'm puzzled by dark rounded holes within intermediate tissue, since if these are also metatarsals I'd expect marrow to appear bright like the earlier slices unless fat suppression is altering the signal. I should just zoom into axial slice 42 to get a clearer look at these structures.

content.text: axial 42/58 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 5/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
I'm trying to figure out what this small structure actually is—skin outer ring, fat layer, branching tissue inside, roughly 30x45mm. The axial slices showing 3-4 round digit-like structures make me wonder if this could be a small foot, possibly from a child, though a heavily downsampled image is also a possibility worth considering.

I'm weighing whether the branching tissue around slices 38-49 with dark round holes represents an infiltrating tumor like fibromatosis versus normal muscle with tendons running through it. Looking at the bright round structures across different planes, I'm trying to work out if these are metatarsal heads lined up along what the display shows as one axis but which might actually correspond to the medial-lateral direction of a foot, which would mean the more proximal slices are showing metatarsal shafts or interosseous muscles instead.

Checking whether the surrounding skin ring encloses dark fat, which would suggest fat-suppressed T2 imaging — if so, the bright round structures could be fluid-filled tendon sheaths or edema rather than solid tumor, since fibrous tumors typically show low-to-intermediate signal instead. I'm also trying to locate the crop center relative to the bright structures to see if the geometry lines up with my foot interpretation, and examining later slices for a homogeneous bright mass that might indicate a distinct pathological lesion.

I'm tracing that bright mass through adjacent slices to see whether it gets cut off at the edge of the volume, and cross-referencing with coronal views to confirm it's the same structure seen from a different plane. Given the central, infiltrative appearance of the intermediate-signal branching tissue, I'm leaning toward a fibromatosis or desmoid-type fibrous tumor and want to trace its full extent on coronal imaging.

content.text: sagittal 41/82 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 6/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking: Looking at the sagittal view, the ill-defined intermediate tissue mass centrally in the upper half matches the branching tissue seen on axial slices 38-49. I'll mark a point at axial 42 in the center of that mass.

version v1 (parent v0) | volume 10.7 mL | components 10 (largest 98.9%; 9 others total 0.1 mL) | extent axial 13–57, coronal 23–64, sagittal 27–50 | change +10.7 mL / 0.0 mL | tool calls 8/40, prompts 1/15 | point add (2 mark(s)) | image: axial 44, coronal 42, sagittal 41 through mask centre (green = new mask, red = removed)

content.thinking: The mask spans axial 13-57 with a volume of 10.7 mL, spreading widely and including bright digit structures, which makes me think the intermediate tissue is continuous rather than a discrete lesion. I'm uncertain though, so I want to check the full coronal view at slice 41 to clarify what's actually abnormal here.

content.text: sheet coronal 30–55/82 (8 slices) | v1 | tool calls 9/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
That large bone-containing region can't be right since the mask extends to the top of the volume, which wouldn't happen with an actual lesion. I'm reconsidering whether the lesion is instead the intermediate tissue in a narrower slice range, or possibly a different bright, lobulated structure visible near a digit in one of the axial slices.

Looking more carefully, the small diameter of the digits (~6-8mm) suggests this is actually an infant's hand or foot rather than an adult's, which opens up the possibility of pediatric fibrous tumors like infantile digital fibromatosis or fibrous hamartoma of infancy. The bright regions I'm seeing around the metacarpal/metatarsal heads are likely just normal bright epiphyseal cartilage in an infant, not pathology, so I need to distinguish real lesion from normal pediatric anatomy as I map through the slices.

I'm trying to figure out which side is plantar, since that side would have more soft tissue like intrinsic muscles and fat, suggesting the intermediate tissue could be plantar muscle or fibromatosis. This pattern—infiltrative branching tissue interspersed with fat—actually fits well with fibrous hamartoma of infancy or infantile fibromatosis.

So the real target seems to be this intermediate infiltrative tissue spanning roughly axial slices 35-52, but my current mask has leaked into the bright cartilaginous bones, which I need to exclude. I'm thinking I should restart with a more constrained approach, possibly adding negative points on the bright bony structures, and check axial slices 49 and 53 to pinpoint exactly where the intermediate tissue ends and the bright tarsal bones begin—since the coronal mask seems to have picked up those superior bones incorrectly. I'll examine axial slices 36 and 50 before deciding whether to undo and try a box or lasso approach across multiple slices instead.

content.text: axial 50/58 | crop full | marks fine | overlay outline | v1 | tool calls 10/40, prompts 1/15

content.thinking:
I'm trying to match up the bright lobulated structures with dark centers across slices — likely cartilaginous epiphyses with ossification centers — and figure out whether the dark holes at adjacent levels are the proximal continuation of those same bony structures or something else entirely.

So that resolves to ossified diaphyses appearing dark on fat-sat T2, with bright cartilage at the metaphyseal bases, consistent with normal infant metatarsal anatomy. I'm now trying to pin down what the intermediate-signal tissue represents — possibly plantar intrinsic muscles — by comparing its distribution across several axial levels and cross-referencing against a sagittal slice, though the sagittal view isn't adding much clarity given the uncertainty in aligning indices between planes.

Given this, I'm leaning toward the intermediate infiltrative tissue being the best candidate for a fibrous hamartoma pattern, so I want to refine my mask to isolate it while excluding the bright cartilage, likely by placing negative points on the bright structures at axial slice 50.

content.text: version v2 (parent v1) | volume 5.3 mL | components 5 (largest 99.9%; 4 others total 0.0 mL) | extent axial 25–57, coronal 25–61, sagittal 34–48 | change +0.0 mL / -5.4 mL | tool calls 11/40, prompts 2/15 | point erase (4 mark(s)) | image: axial 43, coronal 44, sagittal 43 through mask centre (green = new mask, red = removed)

content.thinking: The mask still picks up bright regions around axial 28-30, likely metatarsal heads, extending up to slice 57, and the intermediate tissue in sagittal slice 43 covers the upper half, which feels too uncertain. With the mask now at about 5.3 mL and mostly intermediate tissue, I want to check the top slices around axial 53-57 to see what's actually there.

content.text: sheet axial 25–57/58 (12 slices) | v2 | tool calls 12/40, prompts 2/15

content.thinking:
I'm tracking the lobulated intermediate-signal tissue across axial slices, trying to figure out if it's continuous with the muscle near the metatarsal heads or a separate structure.

I'm considering whether the dark, round holes lateral to the intermediate column could be flexor tendons rather than part of the bone or interosseous tissue, since tendons would appear dark on T2 while red marrow in infant metatarsal shafts would appear intermediate.

So the column is likely metatarsals with normal red marrow, and the brighter region beyond it is tarsal cartilage — meaning my mask was tracking normal bone, not a lesion. I need to look elsewhere for asymmetry: there's a bright lobulated structure near a toe around axial 15-19, possibly epiphyseal cartilage, and another intermediate lobulated mass around axial 54-57 that could be a better candidate for the actual abnormality.

That dorsal lobulated tissue could just be extensor digitorum brevis, so I'm not convinced yet. Considering pediatric soft-tissue fibrous tumors like infantile digital fibromatosis or fibrous hamartoma as possibilities, I want to scan through the toe slices 8-24 more carefully.

content.text: sheet axial 8–27/58 (10 slices) | v2 | tool calls 13/40, prompts 2/15

content.thinking:
At axial slices 12-19, I notice the third toe has a bright crescent-shaped mass wrapped around its plantar/lateral surface, distinct from the other toes—a lobulated bright lesion spanning roughly axial 11-21 that could represent something like infantile digital fibromatosis, though the T2 brightness is a bit atypical for that diagnosis.

I also see the big toe at 14-19 has an internal bright region, which is probably the cartilage epiphysis rather than a lesion, while the third toe's bright crescent sits externally against the bone ring. There's some ambiguity at axial 12-14 about whether the bright area is purely external or extends into the toe's interior, but I'll go with the crescent mass interpretation and cross-check it against v0 and the segmentation at axial 16.

content.text:
Final review of v3: volume 1.3 mL | components 1 (largest 100.0%) | extent axial 10–24, coronal 31–45, sagittal 34–48 | tool calls 18/40, prompts 3/15. The image shows five slices per plane (three inside the mask extent + one just past each end; past-the-mask panels are orange). Check: (1) Is lesion tissue visible in the past-the-mask panels (orange)? Then the mask stops too early: seg_view that slice and add positive points on the lesion there. (2) Does the outline cut through lesion or include normal tissue on any panel? (3) Stray components? If any answer shows a problem, fix it before finishing. Candidates (second image): automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only (often wrong).
C1 add 3.7 mL, does not touch the mask, mostly superior of the mask
C2 add 2.9 mL, touches mask on its posterior, left and inferior sides, mostly superior of the mask
C3 add 2.8 mL, does not touch the mask, mostly superior of the mask
candidate image: one row per candidate, columns axial / coronal / sagittal through the candidate (green outline = current mask, magenta outline + light tint = candidate; judge the tissue inside the magenta outline). For each candidate decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept) or normal tissue (reject). Accept with seg_accept and call seg_finish again for a new review; if none belong, confirm with the review code. If everything is right, call seg_finish again with review_code "8984" to save it.

content.thinking: These candidates look like normal tissue, and the mask seems reasonable, so I'm done.

arguments.reason: Bright lobulated mass encasing one toe; boundary fits in all planes, lesion identity somewhat uncertain

content.thinking: I should be upfront about my uncertainty here, particularly around whether the phalanx is actually included and any identity questions that remain unresolved.

content.text:
I saved a mask, but I'm only moderately sure it covers the right structure (confidence marked medium). It outlines a bright, lobulated mass wrapped around one toe; the final version is v3.

**What I segmented:** one connected region of about 1.3 mL, spanning axial slices 10–24. The scan looks like an infant's forefoot. One toe stood out from the others: it is enlarged and has a bright rim plus a bulging lobule on one side, which none of the other toes show. In the final review the outline fit this mass in all three planes. The candidate check proposed three additions, but they were metatarsals, cartilage and normal soft tissue, so I left them out.

**Why the confidence isn't higher:**
- **Signal intensity:** fibrous tumors are usually low-to-intermediate on T2, and this mass is bright. I chose it because it is the only clear left–right difference in the volume, not because it looks typically fibrous.
- **Bone may be included:** the mask probably contains the toe's own bone along with the tumor around it. The tumor seems to encircle the bone and I couldn't reliably separate the two, so the volume may be slightly too large.
- **An earlier wrong target:** my first try was the branching intermediate-signal tissue in the mid-foot (axial slices ~37–50). On a closer look it is normal anatomy, most likely the metatarsals with tendons beside them, so I discarded it.

The case used 19 of 40 tool calls and 3 of 15 model prompts.
